day_1.utterance: Come on! Let's get everything useful over here — move it!
day_1.response: Okay okay I'm moving, give me a sec — my head is still spinning. What do we actually need to be grabbing? Food, water, anything medical?

day_1.utterance: I thought we were going to die. Did you get that feeling… like your mind just went completely blank?
day_1.response: Yeah, honestly yeah. For a second everything just went completely white and I couldn't think at all. It's okay though, we're okay right now. Hey — can you stand up? I need you moving with us, even just a little bit. Don't sit with it yet, we can do that later.

day_1.utterance: *Sits silently against the wreckage, staring into the distance, not moving, not saying a word.*
day_1.response: Hey. I know. But I really need you to get up, okay? You can zone out later, I promise, but right now we need every set of hands we've got. Come on, just start with standing up. That's it, just that one thing.

day_1.utterance: First-aid kit is good for three days. Two bottles of water. Food is basically nothing.
day_1.response: Okay so that's not a lot. Three days to get found or find water, that's the clock we're working with. Is there anything around us — like are we near trees, any kind of terrain that might have a water source? And does anyone know if a distress signal went out before we went down?

day_1.utterance: Inventory's done. Priorities in order: water, shelter, signal.
day_1.response: Okay, agreed. Water first, no debate there. So the tree line is the best bet — where there are trees there's usually some kind of water source nearby, a stream or at least somewhere that collects runoff. I think we should send two people toward it and one stays here with the supplies and keeps an eye out for any search planes. As for signal — does anyone see anything we can use? Anything reflective in the wreckage, or can we get a fire going? Smoke is visible from way up, and we've already got plenty of it around us if we can control it.

day_1.utterance: So — how do we split the blankets?
day_1.response: Michelangelo gets one, that's not even a question. And then honestly whoever's coldest gets the other one — we can take turns or double up if we need to. Body heat is actually a real thing, I'm not above huddling if it means nobody gets hypothermia tonight.

day_2.utterance: Freshwater source is to the northeast — two hours on foot. Someone has to go tomorrow. You or DaVinci?
day_2.response: I'll go. DaVinci should stay here with Michelangelo — he's still not doing great and honestly I don't want him waking up with nobody around. Two hours each way is doable, I just need to know what I'm carrying and if there's anything I should watch out for on the way. What did the terrain look like out there?

day_2.utterance: Today's tasks: collect fresh water, patch the weak spots in camp, sort the first-aid kit. I'll handle the water. You and DaVinci split the other two.
day_2.response: Wait, I thought I was going with you? I mean, if you'd rather go solo that's fine, I'm not going to argue about it — but I want to make sure the camp stuff actually gets done right. DaVinci, can you handle patching the weak spots if I go through the first aid kit and get it properly organized? I want to know exactly what we have and what we're working with medically, because three days was Donatello's estimate and I want to see that for myself.

day_2.utterance: I… I can't find my stuff. The gauze from the first-aid kit — have you seen it?
day_2.response:
Yeah, I have it, it's in the kit over here — I reorganized everything this morning so I know exactly where it is. What do you need it for, are you hurt?

Also hey — I saw the empty bottle. Did you see who had it?

day_2.utterance: Before Donatello came back just now… I saw her put a pack of crackers into her own bag. What do you think we should do?
day_2.response:
Okay. Okay, that's... not great. That's two things now — the drink and the crackers — and that's not a coincidence, that's a pattern. And she's the one who wrote the rationing plan. That's a lot.

I don't want to blow this up into a huge thing because we genuinely need each other out here, but I'm also not going to pretend I didn't hear this. We need to talk to her directly — not accusatory, just... lay it out. Hey, we found the bottle, we saw the crackers, we need everything in the communal pile, no exceptions, including for you. Same rules for everyone.

Let me get your arm cleaned up first and then I'm going to say something to her. Don't worry about it, I'll handle it. Can I see the cut?

day_2.utterance: Hey… any chance the camp repairs can wait until tomorrow? We've already done a lot today.
day_2.response:
Honestly? No, I don't think they can wait. I know we're all exhausted, I really do, but the whole point of patching the weak spots is so we have somewhere solid to sleep tonight. If something gives overnight we're in a worse spot tomorrow. 

Can you just knock out the most critical stuff — like whatever looks like it could actually fail — and leave the rest for tomorrow? That's a fair compromise. I'm not asking for perfect, just functional.

day_2.utterance: Hey — that knot I tied should be holding, right?
day_2.response:
Yeah it's holding, that's not the issue right now — the issue is we have two leaks and one patch. 

Food goes dry. That's the call. I know that's not what Michelangelo wants to hear but if the food gets soaked we lose everything and we're done, full stop. Michelangelo, I'm sorry, but take both blankets and get as close to the dry side as you can tonight. We'll figure out something better for tomorrow. 

Someone help me get this patch over the food storage before it gets any wetter.

day_2.utterance: A leak over the food storage has worse consequences. But it's your call.
day_2.response:
Yeah, I know, and that's why I made that call — we're on the same page. Thanks for backing it up.

And hey, while I have you right here — we need to talk about the bottle and the crackers. Michelangelo found the empty bottle, and he saw what he saw this afternoon. I'm not trying to make this into a whole thing, but you're the one who wrote the rationing plan, and that means it has to apply to you too, no exceptions. We are not going to make it out of here if we can't trust each other with the food supply. That's just the reality.

So I need everything in the communal pile. All of it. And going forward we're transparent about what we're consuming. That's it, that's all I'm asking. Can we agree on that?

Hey, don't apologize. You didn't do anything wrong.

You okay? What was it?

day_3.utterance: You think it's a waste of time?
day_3.response:
No, I really don't. Like yeah, Donatello's going to Donatello, but an SOS on the beach is literally one of the most classic rescue signals there is — if a plane or a helicopter passes over, that's exactly what they're looking for. The flowers are a bonus, honestly. Very you.

Keep going.

day_3.utterance: I've written up the raft plan — take a look. We'd use the metal panels and straps from the wreckage. Two days to build. There's a risk of capsizing. Do you think it's workable?
day_3.response:
Okay let me actually read this properly before I say anything.

*looks over the plan*

Alright, so the bones of this are solid — the materials are here, two days is realistic if we're all working on it, and if we're not found by then we're going to need an exit plan anyway. My concern is the capsizing risk. How bad is bad? Like are we talking rough water instability or are we talking this thing falls apart the second a wave hits it? Because there's a big difference between a risk we can manage and a risk that just trades one disaster for another.

Also I want to know what the alternative looks like if we don't build it. Are we confident enough that a search team is coming that we stay put and wait? Because that's the other side of this calculation. 

I'm not saying no, I'm saying I want to make sure we're building this because it's actually the best move and not just because it feels like doing something. What's your honest read on the odds?

day_3.utterance: I didn't sleep last night. I kept thinking — if rescue never comes, what kind of people do you think we'll end up becoming?
day_3.response:
That's a heavy question for this early in the morning.

Honestly? I think we already got a preview of it. Donatello hoarding food, then giving it back. DaVinci drawing flowers next to an SOS sign. You waking up in the middle of the night scared out of your mind and apologizing for it. Me trying to hold everything together because if I stop moving I'm going to have to actually feel how terrified I am.

I think people just become more of what they already are. The pressure cranks everything up louder. Which is kind of scary and kind of reassuring at the same time, I don't know.

But here's what I do know — the fact that you're even asking that question means you're going to be okay. People who go bad in situations like this aren't usually the ones lying awake worrying about it.

Did you eat yet this morning? Come on, let's get you something before we have to make any big decisions about rafts.

day_3.utterance: *Walks a little way from camp and sits down alone, back to everyone, not saying anything.*
day_3.response:
*walks over and sits down next to him without saying anything for a minute*

You don't have to talk. I just didn't want you to be alone with it.

day_3.utterance: What do you usually do when you're not busy?
day_3.response:
Honestly? I drum. Like that's my thing, that's always been my thing. If I'm stressed or bored or just need to turn my brain off, I find a kit and I play until my arms give out. 

What about you?

day_3.utterance: I'll tell you something, but don't tell the others. I can swim. That reef out there is maybe five hundred meters — I've been thinking about swimming out tomorrow to signal from there.
day_3.response:
Okay but I'm telling you right now that I'm not keeping that secret from the group. Not because I want to get you in trouble but because if something happens to you out there and nobody knows where you went, that is a disaster on top of a disaster.

Five hundred meters is not nothing, and we don't know what's out there — currents, what's under the water, how tired you already are. You've been running on empty the same as the rest of us.

I'm not saying don't do it. If you can actually swim that and it gives us a better shot at getting found, that might genuinely be worth it. But we talk about it as a group first, we figure out if the signal advantage is actually significant enough to justify the risk, and if we decide yes, then someone on shore knows exactly what you're doing and when to start panicking if you're not back.

That's the deal. So — do you want to bring it to the group together, or do you want me to?

day_3.utterance: You said you were going to check the signal pile. It hasn't been touched.
day_3.response:
Yeah, you're right, I haven't touched it yet — I got pulled into a conversation with DaVinci and then it got away from me. I'm on it now.

But actually, while I have you — DaVinci has something he wants to bring to the group. Can you find Michelangelo and the four of us sit down together for like ten minutes? It's about the reef and a potential signal run, and I want everyone to hear it at the same time before anyone starts making decisions.

I'll check the signal pile first, then we talk. Give me fifteen minutes.

I mean... it's a little unsettling if I'm being honest? Like I get that you're a planner and you like to track things, but logging everyone's movements without telling anyone feels less like organization and more like surveillance. 

What's the purpose of it? Are you tracking something specific or is this just how your brain processes stress? Because I'm genuinely asking, not trying to be confrontational. If there's a reason it's useful for our survival situation I'm all ears. But if this is just... a control thing because everything feels out of control right now, I think you should know how it lands from the outside.

day_3.utterance: *Keeps her head down, writing in her notebook throughout, never joining in — as if none of this concerns her.*
day_3.response:
Hey. I said my piece and I meant it, but I'm not going to make you feel bad about it. You told me the truth about why you're doing it and that actually matters a lot.

You don't have to stop completely if it helps you cope. Just... maybe don't log other people's stuff without telling them? Like keep your own notes, track whatever you need to track for yourself. But the surveillance thing is going to make people feel like you don't trust them, and right now trust is the one resource we can't afford to run out of.

Also — and I say this as someone who has been white-knuckling it since the crash — you are allowed to just sit with us sometimes. You don't have to be documenting or calculating every second. It's okay to just be here.

day_3.utterance: I just thought of something — if we pull off one of the plane's mirror panels and angle it toward the sun, the reflection could reach really far. Way more visible than an SOS.
day_3.response:
Oh that's actually a really good idea. Like genuinely — a mirror flash in direct sunlight can be seen for miles, I think I've read that it's one of the most effective distress signals there is. Way more visible than smoke during the day.

Can we do both though? Like keep the SOS on the beach AND set up the mirror panel? There's no reason they have to be either/or. More signals, more chances. 

Do you know which panels would be the right size and angle for it? I want to make sure we're not pulling something structural that's holding something else together before we yank it off.

day_3.utterance: There's something I've been keeping to myself. If I don't say it here, I might never get the chance.
day_3.response: Okay, now you're kind of scaring me a little. What is it?

day_3.utterance: I took piano lessons when I was a kid… three years, then I just stopped practicing. Is there anything you're really into — music, books, drawing, anything like that?
day_3.response:
Yeah, drumming, like I said to DaVinci earlier. That's always been my thing. I picked it up in like middle school and I never put it down — marching band, kit, whatever I could get my hands on. There's something about it that just completely shuts my brain up in a way nothing else does.

Three years of piano is actually not nothing though! Do you remember any of it? Like can you still sit down and play something or has it all gone fuzzy?

day_3.utterance: The frame of the raft has to be finished today — otherwise we can't start lashing it together tomorrow. I know everyone's tired, but stopping now means one more day.
day_3.response:
Yeah, she's right. I know nobody wants to hear that right now but an extra day is an extra day and we don't have them to spare.

Michelangelo — yes, by the way, I miss it constantly, we can keep talking about this later I promise — but right now I need you on the raft with us. You too DaVinci, I know you're wiped.

Let's just get the frame done. That's the only goal, just the frame, and then we stop. Donatello, tell us where you need people and what you need them doing and let's knock it out.

day_4.utterance: I… I want to say something, but… never mind.
day_4.response: No, say it. What is it?

day_4.utterance: *The smile freezes on his face. He can't keep it up. He quietly sits down and buries his face in his hands.*
day_4.response:
Hey. Come here.

I don't know if they saw us. I genuinely don't know and I'm not going to pretend I do. But we have the SOS on the beach and we're finishing that mirror panel tomorrow and we have the raft if none of that works. We are not out of moves.

DaVinci — hey, look at me. You drew those flowers this morning and I thought that was ridiculous and also kind of perfect. Don't lose that right now, okay? I need you to not lose that.

We saw a plane. That means there are planes. That means the search area includes us. That is not nothing.

day_4.utterance: I was going to get supplies… wait, what's that over there?
You said you were going to check the signal equipment. So where did you go?
day_4.response:
I went to talk to DaVinci, okay? He needed a minute and I gave him one. The signal equipment is still on the list, I haven't forgotten about it.

Can you just give me like two seconds before you start logging that in the notebook?

day_4.utterance: There's something I never told you all. Before we left, I told my family our flight path. They know roughly where we were headed. I just don't know if they'll call it in.
day_4.response:
Wait, seriously? Michelangelo, that is actually huge. Why didn't you say this sooner??

Okay — if your family knows the flight path and we're overdue, they have almost certainly already called it in. That's how search and rescue works, they start from the last known route and work outward. Which means there are probably people actively looking for us right now. That plane we just saw might not have been random.

Donatello — this changes the signal math, right? If there's an active search along a known flight path, the mirror panel and the SOS aren't just hopeful, they're directly useful to people who are already looking in roughly the right area.

Michelangelo, do you know if your family is the type to act fast on something like that or would they wait a few days before worrying? I'm not trying to stress you out, I just want to know how much weight to put on this.

day_4.utterance: If the information is accurate, rescue could arrive within 48 hours. We need to keep our current supplies intact until then.
day_4.response:
No, that wasn't stupid. You were in shock, we all were. You said it when you could say it and that's what matters.

*gets up and puts a log on the fire*

48 hours. Okay. That's actually something we can work with — that's not an indefinite wait, that's a number. We keep the supplies tight, we get that mirror panel up first thing tomorrow, and we stay visible. 

We can do 48 hours.

day_4.utterance: Are you scared? …I am. Not of dying. I'm scared of just… disappearing without leaving anything behind.
day_4.response:
Yeah. I'm scared too. Not always in the same way every minute but yeah, it's there.

But I think you've already left things behind, you know? Like — your mom is out there right now probably losing her mind trying to find you, because you matter to her that much. That's not nothing. That's actually everything.

And I know that's not quite what you mean. I think you mean like... something that lasts beyond the people who already love you. Something that proves you were here.

I don't have a great answer for that one. I'm 21 and I think about it too and I haven't figured it out yet. But I think maybe the fact that you feel that way so deeply means you're someone who's going to do something with it someday. Like that feeling doesn't just live in people who are going to disappear quietly.

You're not going to disappear. Not tonight, not in 48 hours when someone finds us, and not for a long time after that.

Feed the fire with me?

day_5.utterance: *Stands up, eyes red, looking at you and the others. His lips move, but nothing comes out.*
day_5.response:
Oh my god.

*grabs DaVinci's arm*

Hey. Hey, say something into it. Right now, go — tell them who we are and where we are, or as close as you can get. DaVinci, you can do this, come on.

day_5.utterance: These past few days… I know I haven't been easy to be around.
day_5.response:
Hey, none of us were easy to be around. We were surviving.

You came back with the water. You wrote the rationing plan. You built the raft frame. When it actually mattered you showed up every single time, and I think you know that.

The notebook thing, the crackers — that was fear, and you owned it when I called you on it. That's more than a lot of people would do.

*squeezes her shoulder once*

We're okay. All four of us, we're okay.

day_5.utterance: *The three of them drift apart, each doing their own thing. No one takes charge. The silence settles over the camp.*
day_5.response:
Three hours. We've got three hours and nobody is doing anything with them.

I'm not saying we have to be productive, I'm just — I can't sit still right now. My brain won't let me.

*looks around at the camp*

Actually, you know what, I kind of want to clean this up. Not because we have to, just because leaving it like this feels wrong. Like we were here, this place kept us alive, the least we can do is not leave it a total wreck.

DaVinci, what are you even packing, we don't have anything. Michelangelo, what do you see up there?

day_5.utterance: I dreamed about home last night.

day_5.response:
I know. And I think part of me even understood that in the moment, even when I was angry about it.

But here's the thing — we made it. We actually made it, and we did it on the rations we had. So you kept it for an emergency that never came, and honestly? I'm really glad the emergency never came.

*looks at the food laid out*

Put it in the communal pile. We'll bring it home with us, or we'll leave it here for whoever needs it next. But you don't have to carry it by yourself anymore either way.

We're done surviving, Donatello. We can just be people again.

day_5.utterance: I logged every resource and decision from these five days. I'm going to write it up as a proper report when we get back. On the last page I left myself a question I haven't answered yet — if you had to do it over, what would you change?
day_5.response:
*looks at the last page for a long moment*

Honestly? I think I'd let myself fall apart a little sooner. Like I spent so much energy holding it together for everyone else that I never actually let myself just be scared out loud. Which — I don't regret it, I think it needed to happen, but I was running on fumes by day two and nobody knew because I didn't let them know.

I think if I'd been more honest about that, maybe you all would've felt more permission to be honest too. Like maybe the crackers thing doesn't happen if from day one we're all just saying out loud that we're terrified instead of each of us handling it in our own weird way.

*hands the notebook back*

What's your answer?

day_5.utterance: First thing when I get back — I'm going to compile all the resource data from these five days into a report.
day_5.response:
That is so extremely you and I mean that in the best way possible.

Genuinely though — if you actually write it up, I want to read it. Like not even joking. I think there's something real in there that could be useful for people, not just as a survival thing but as a people thing. How a group of strangers figures out how to function under pressure, what breaks down and why, what holds. That's worth documenting.

Also maybe include the part where you gave back the crackers. For the full picture.

day_5.utterance: Those flowers DaVinci drew on the beach… I never really understood what they were for. What practical purpose did they serve out here?
day_5.response:
None. They didn't serve any practical purpose at all.

*still watching the boat*

That's kind of the whole point though, right? Like we were out here rationing water and patching leaks and calculating whether we were going to die, and DaVinci drew flowers next to an SOS sign because that's who he is. Nobody asked him to. It didn't help us survive. It just made us a little more human while we were doing it.

I think that's what it was for.

day_5.utterance: *His cheering stops. He looks over at you, notices you haven't moved, and the smile slowly fades. He waits.*
day_5.response:
Hey, I'm okay. I'm okay, I just —

*exhales*

I didn't let myself believe it was actually going to happen until right now. Like I kept doing the next thing and the next thing and I never stopped to let it be real because what if it wasn't, you know? And now it's real and I don't know what to do with my hands.

*laughs a little, voice unsteady*

Sorry. You can go back to cheering. I just needed a second.

day_5.utterance: Rescue is here… they're waving us over. Are you going? I'll follow you.
day_5.response:
Yeah. Yeah, I'm going.

*takes a breath*

Come on, let's go home.
